name: Exosome facial
lead: An exosome facial is an aesthetic procedure in which a product marketed as containing exosomes, small membrane-enclosed vesicles released by cells, is applied to or introduced into the facial skin, commonly after microneedling or laser treatment, with the aim of improving skin quality, texture and scarring. [1][2] Exosomes are one subtype of extracellular vesicle, and the source cells for aesthetic products vary: mesenchymal stem cells, adipose tissue, umbilical cord, and plants have all been named in trial registrations. [3][4][5]

The look people want is smoother, more even, firmer-looking skin and fewer visible acne scars, with downtime that is shorter than a laser alone. Proponents describe exosomes as signalling messengers that nudge skin cells toward repair, and clinics offer them as an add-on to microneedling, radiofrequency microneedling or fractional laser, which open channels in the skin surface.[2][6][10]

In looksmaxxing and aesthetic-clinic circles the treatment is positioned as a next-generation alternative to platelet-rich plasma and similar regenerative procedures. Published evidence is early: the entries found are small registered studies, many with 7 to 40 participants, and several are listed as completed without published results in the record reviewed.[6][7][8]

The wider context is the regenerative-aesthetics market. Platelet-rich plasma facials, popularised in the 2010s partly through celebrity endorsement and often combined with microneedling, set the template of a biological product placed after skin needling, and exosome products are marketed as a cell-free successor to that approach [19][20]. Clinics also offer exosomes in skincare under cosmetic labels, and Wikipedia reports that some firms describe their products as 'minimally manipulated' while the FDA maintains that review is required [18].

The US Food and Drug Administration stated in a 2019 public safety notification that no exosome products were FDA-approved, and reported serious adverse events in patients treated with unapproved exosome-labelled products in Nebraska. [9]

paras: Exosomes are vesicles formed inside cells and released when an internal compartment fuses with the cell membrane. Wikipedia's article on extracellular vesicles notes that the word has been used inconsistently and that 'extracellular vesicle' is the preferred term unless a particular origin has been shown. [10] Vesicles can carry RNA between cells, and much of the research on their regenerative or anti-aging potential comes from cell culture and animal models. [10]

Wikipedia's exosome article describes vesicles of roughly 30 to 150 nanometres that form when late endosomes bud inward and then fuse with the cell membrane, carrying proteins, lipids and nucleic acids such as mRNA and microRNA that reflect the cell of origin. It adds that whether exosomal RNA actually changes recipient cells in mammals is still debated, and that the field increasingly prefers the term extracellular vesicle unless an endosomal origin has been shown.[10][18]

In aesthetic practice, exosome products are described as being applied topically following a skin-penetrating step such as microneedling, radiofrequency microneedling or fractional laser, or injected into the skin. Registered studies describe combinations with microneedling devices, fractional CO2 laser, Q-switched laser, and subcision. [2][3][6][7][11]

The marketing vocabulary overlaps: 'exosomes', 'extracellular vesicles', 'secretome', 'biosomes' and 'conditioned media' appear in product and trial names, and they are not always interchangeable [6][7][10]. Wikipedia's exosome article reports that functional RNA transfer between mammalian cells is still described as limited evidence, and that RNA found in vesicles does not necessarily have a biological role [18].

Wikipedia traces exosomes to work on maturing reticulocytes: two groups reported them in 1983, the Johnstone group named them exosomes in 1987, and the term had been used more loosely for extracellular vesicles by Trams and colleagues in 1981.[18] Research interest has since covered cancer vaccines, drug delivery and wound healing; the same article says some clinics market exosomes in skincare with wrinkle-reduction claims and that the FDA considers cosmetic or therapeutic use to need review and approval.[18]

Wikipedia's exosome article adds that the mRNA and microRNA cargo of exosomes was first reported at the University of Gothenburg, with a 2007 citation [18]. The aesthetic use followed a decade of research on mesenchymal stem cells, whose benefits in tissue repair some researchers came to attribute to secreted vesicles rather than the cells themselves; reviews of this idea in the late 2010s and early 2020s include work on skin regeneration and wound healing [18].

In December 2019 the FDA issued its public safety notification, and Wikipedia reports that in 2020 the agency also warned several firms about marketing exosomes for COVID-19 and other conditions [9][18].

Clinics describe the product as a vial of vesicles derived from mesenchymal stem cells, adipose tissue, umbilical cord or plants, applied topically after a skin-penetrating step or injected into the skin.[2][3][4][5] Registered studies name pairings with microneedling devices, radiofrequency microneedling, fractional CO2 laser, Q-switched laser and subcision, and indications include general skin quality, wrinkles, skin tone and atrophic acne scars.[2][3][6][7][11][15] Product sources and preparation vary between providers, and the FDA says some clinics offer exosome products outside the premarket review process.[9]

Exosome treatments grew out of the stem-cell and PRP clinics of the 2010s. Platelet-rich plasma, usually combined with microneedling in so-called vampire facials, became popular during that decade largely through celebrity endorsement; Wikipedia notes that evidence for PRP is mixed across conditions, strongest in dermatology for hair loss, and that its use is off-label because the FDA does not regulate PRP itself [20]. Exosomes were positioned as a product that needs no blood draw and no live cells.

Wikipedia's exosome article reports that US clinics have marketed exosome products for anti-aging, joint pain and other conditions, often alongside non-approved stem-cell injections, and that others sell exosomes in skincare under cosmetic labels [18]. Aesthetic-clinic menus describe the treatment as 'exosome microneedling', 'exosome facial' or 'secretome facial', and the registered studies reflect the same range of pairings [2][7][13].
The treatment appears mainly through clinic marketing and clinical trial registrations rather than through a defined forum doctrine.

In general terms, the skin is prepared with a needling or laser step, the exosome product is applied, and recovery follows the needling or laser step [2][3]. Practitioners describe sessions as part of a series paired with the underlying device. Microneedling itself is a cosmetic procedure that punctures the skin repeatedly with sterile needles and is used for scarring and acne [19]. The procedure is performed by clinicians and not described here as a home practice.

Closest relatives are microneedling with topical serums, platelet-rich plasma facials, radiofrequency microneedling, fractional laser resurfacing, subcision and hyaluronic acid fillers for scars, all of which appear in the registered exosome studies [3][5][7][15][19][20]. Safety issues documented for PRP-microneedling include the April 2024 CDC report of three women diagnosed with HIV after vampire facials at an unlicensed Albuquerque spa; investigators found the operator was unlicensed and reused blood-contaminated single-use equipment [19][20].

A search of ClinicalTrials.gov finds a cluster of small, recent registrations. They include a 30-participant phase 4 study of topical exosomes applied with a microneedling device for facial skin aging (completed, started 2024) [2], a 20-participant phase 3 study combining laser and exosomes for skin rejuvenation (completed, started 2025) [11], and a 12-participant study of AnteAGE exosomes with microneedling for facial skin quality [12]. A 30-participant study examined AnteAGE biosomes with radiofrequency microneedling for rejuvenation, wrinkles and skin tone [13], and a 7-participant proof-of-concept study examined a secretome/exosome serum for cosmetic improvement [14].

Several registrations concern atrophic acne scars: a 12-participant pilot combining subcision, adipose-derived exosomes and powdered polydioxanone [15]; a 22-participant study of umbilical-cord and bone-marrow stem-cell-derived exosomes [16]; and a 30-participant study comparing fractional CO2 laser with plant-derived exosomes against non-cross-linked hyaluronic acid [17]. A 38-participant study observed exosomes after Q-switched laser surgery [3], and a 40-participant phase 3 study of intradermal stem-cell-derived exosomes on facial skin quality is registered as not yet recruiting. [1]

The registrations reviewed do not themselves report outcomes, and the studies are small. No large randomized controlled trial or systematic review of exosome facials was identified in the sources consulted.

In December 2019 the FDA stated that there were no FDA-approved exosome products, that exosomes used to treat diseases in humans are generally regulated as drugs and biological products requiring premarket review, and that some clinics offer exosome products outside that process. [9] The agency reported multiple serious adverse events among patients in Nebraska treated with unapproved products marketed as containing exosomes, and asked health professionals and consumers to report adverse events through MedWatch. [9]

The notice advises US patients to ask whether the FDA has reviewed a treatment and to request its investigational new drug (IND) number, and advises people considering treatment abroad to learn the local regulations and take care, since the FDA has limited oversight of foreign treatments. [9] It is addressed to patients, practitioners and clinics, and notes that some clinics marketing stem-cell products also offer exosome treatments with claims the agency calls unsubstantiated. [9]

Wikipedia's exosome article reports that critics warn of risks such as inflammation, infection and serious injury from unapproved products, and that clinics reportedly promote exosomes for several conditions despite limited clinical evidence [18]. The FDA's notice also says clinics' assertions that these products fall outside drug and biologic rules are incorrect [9].

timeline.event: Trams and colleagues use the term exosome for extracellular vesicles.[18]
The Johnstone group names exosomes in maturing reticulocytes.[18]
First report of mRNA and microRNA cargo in exosomes, from the University of Gothenburg (per Wikipedia's citation).[18]
FDA issues a public safety notification stating no exosome products are approved and reporting serious adverse events in Nebraska. [9]
FDA warns several firms about marketing exosomes for COVID-19 and other conditions.[18]
Start of a registered observational study of exosomes after Q-switched laser surgery. [3]
CDC reports HIV in three women after vampire facials at an unlicensed spa, a safety event in the neighbouring PRP-microneedling field.[19][20]
Start of registered studies of exosomes with microneedling and radiofrequency microneedling. [2][13]
Several small registered studies of exosomes with laser or microneedling begin. [11][12][16][17]

lore.intro: Exosome facials are discussed mainly in aesthetic-clinic marketing and early trial registrations, as a next step beyond PRP and microneedling for skin quality and acne scars.

claims.claim: Exosomes act as repair signals that improve skin texture and tone
claims.believers: Proponents describe exosomes as messengers that nudge skin cells toward repair, giving smoother, brighter skin.[2][10]
claims.experts: Much of the supporting research is from cell culture and animal models, and Wikipedia says functional RNA transfer between mammalian cells is still limited in evidence.[10][18] Registered human studies are small.[2][11]

claims.claim: Exosomes added after microneedling or laser improve acne scars
claims.believers: Clinics pair exosomes with subcision, fractional CO2 laser or microneedling for atrophic acne scars.[15][16][17]
claims.experts: Registered studies of 12 to 30 participants compare combinations; the registrations reviewed report no outcomes.[15][16][17]

claims.claim: Exosomes shorten downtime compared with laser alone
claims.believers: Providers describe adding exosomes after laser or microneedling to support recovery.[3]
claims.experts: A 38-participant registered study observes exosomes after Q-switched laser surgery; outcomes were not reported in the record reviewed.[3]

claims.claim: Exosomes are a cell-free alternative to PRP
claims.believers: Clinics offer exosomes as a successor to PRP and 'vampire' facials without a blood draw.[20]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes PRP evidence as mixed and strongest for hair loss; no head-to-head exosome trials were identified.[20]

claims.claim: Exosome products fall outside drug rules
claims.believers: Some firms describe products as 'minimally manipulated' or cosmetic.[18]
claims.experts: The FDA states that exosomes used to treat disease are regulated as drugs and biologics and that no exosome products are approved; it called clinic claims to the contrary false.[9]

claims.claim: Source of the exosomes (stem cell, adipose, umbilical, plant) determines results
claims.believers: Providers differentiate products by origin, such as umbilical-cord, adipose or plant-derived.[3][4][5][16]
claims.experts: Registered studies use different sources and pairings, and product preparation varies between providers; no comparison across sources was found.[4][5][9]

card.summary: Skin-quality treatment using cell-derived vesicles after microneedling or laser: only small early studies exist and no exosome product is FDA-approved.
card.aka: Exosome therapy, exosome microneedling, secretome facial
card.note: FDA reported serious adverse events with unapproved exosome products in 2019.

quick.overview:
An exosome facial applies or injects a product said to contain exosomes, tiny vesicles released by cells, usually after microneedling or laser. It is marketed for skin quality, texture and acne scars.

Evidence so far consists of small registered studies, mostly of 7 to 40 people. No large controlled trial was identified.
quick.mechanism: Exosomes can carry RNA and proteins between cells, and proponents propose that products from stem-cell or other sources signal skin cells to repair tissue. Most supporting research is from cell and animal work.
quick.risks: The FDA stated in 2019 that no exosome products were approved and reported serious adverse events in patients given unapproved exosome-labelled products. Product sources and quality vary between providers.
